inline.s:
To meet in life, how brief the day!
As distant as a storm at night.
While you and I were kept away,
We were as sun hid from our sight.
Written at Random: Four Poems

The wind blows willow blossoms down,
To east and west they drift and flee.
Not that they love to follow round —
They have no self to call their own.

The pheasant in a cage is pent,
With millet fare in goodly store.
How much better in woods to live,
Eating and drinking with the hour.

The leopard hides in southern mist,
And ever dreads the hunter's net.
It is because of his own pelt
That body becomes the mind's regret.

Oil-fed flame lights the traveler by night;
While others gain, the lamp consumes its oil.
Should one not hold his own life dear?
Our substance is but what we were lent.
Remembering the Bamboo Pool at Home Mountain

Ten thousand bamboos shower sunlit rain;
Two pools draw water from the rocky spring.
Since I took leave, full thirty years have passed —
Each day I think of the lotus I planted there.
Qiong Mountain

A wonder-land whose realm is fragrance made;
Pearl Cliff, with hills of jade arrayed.
Men cross over from the sea of dust,
As if they issued through heaven's gate.
Five-Finger Mountain

A single leaf floats beyond the sky;
A thousand peaks fall in the glass.
Who was it waved five fingers wide
And clove the vastness of the void?
Golden Millet Spring

The millet floats in golden flakes;
The spring runs white as jade-bright cream.
I come and hold a single bowl —
Enough to serve the Lord of Emptiness.
Mingchang Pagoda

Qiong's seas unroll the dragon store;
The incense banner lifts to Brahmā's height.
Just look within this burning house —
Green lotuses well from the ground.
General Liu Invites Me to See the Jade Dragon Spring: Two Poems

In what year was chaos hewn apart?
This deep spring opened here in this place.
A man stands leaning on the bounds of space;
The hills come walking into the glass.
Inscribed at the Depths of Ink-Fragrance: Four Poems

Green grasses lie like ribbons of script;
The hidden orchid knots its scent.
In the empty pavilion one sits alone —
The mind has already reached high antiquity.

Bamboo hue creeps green beneath the eaves;
Lotus blossoms mirror red in the water.
Deep in the night cold dew descends —
A man sits within the hidden fragrance.

The hibiscus blooms like brocade unfurled;
Yellow chrysanthemums pile up like coins.
Where the drunken eye is steeped in scent,
Serenely there is the Chan of ease.

Snow presses the plum to open its calyx;
Spring hastens the grass to put forth shoots.
Before the eyes, the business of living —
Who knows it, dwelling in the hills?
Sent to Mr. Li of Jiaodong

Ten thousand miles are not so far;
The inch-wide mind, stilled, is freer yet.
I do not know who thinks of me —
As though how many passes lay between.
Thinking of Ding Youwu, Grand Counselor

Falling leaves, and rain on a thousand hills;
One lone cloud in the cold sky.
I lift my head and let my gaze go free —
Where is the place I do not think of you?
In Praise of Pines: Two Poems

The older the tree, the redder its heart;
The maple, fallen, reddens its leaf.
How pitiable, there in the frost and snow —
A single branch of pine stands all alone.

Its frosty trunk wears dragon scales grown old;
Its windy boughs trail long as horses' tails.
The sound of the surge rings out clear and pure —
A rustling fills the empty hall.
In Praise of Plum Blossom: Two Poems

In the grove the autumn is already late;
Ten thousand trees are stripped and sorely hurt.
Only the cold plum tree remains —
Flying in with fragrance from the snow.

Its snowy hue arrives before the spring;
Its cold scent is purer in the night.
One note from a hidden bird —
And suddenly the dreaming soul takes flight.
In Praise of Bamboo: Five Poems

Cold it scatters a thousand feet of jade;
Purely it sprinkles a whole grove with frost.
Though the dust-bound mind lie heavy still,
Gazing on it, one forgets it all at once.

Soaring, it rides above the clouds;
When the wind rises, dragons roar by night.
Through frost and snow it knows nothing of years —
My true friend in the season of cold.

Its frosty trunk is cold as jade;
Its windy boughs sound like a lute.
One night of rain on the Xiao and Xiang
Drips and shatters a traveler's heart.

Its leaves may fall, but its root holds firm;
Its heart is void, and its joints rise higher.
A whole grove lifts in the cold wind's breath —
In the clear night it keeps the pine's own surge.

By the Qi's bend spring clouds are jade-green;
On the Xiao and Xiang night rain is cold.
By the empty window one listens in quiet —
A soughing of jasper stems on every side.
Rejoicing in Rain: Three Poems

Cool rain sifts down through burning sky;
A gust of wind shakes the forest trees.
Light thunder rolls at the eaves' edge,
Faint and far as an empty valley.

The primal sun burns like a raging fire,
And all that is seems kiln-cast and forged.
Then suddenly wind and rain arrive —
And where has all the scorching gone?

The hills are empty, the spring grown colder;
The summer heat comes and goes no more.
A soughing wind and rain arise —
Hair and bones turn fresh and clear.
Songs from the Mountains: Six Poems

Dust lies beyond three thousand worlds;
The mind outsoars the eighteen dhyānas.
The bell's sound rises in the clear night —
I hear it through, and cannot sleep.

Of sun and moon I know not their going;
This mind should rightfully merge with emptiness.
At times I sit alone in the mountain tower,
As if back in the formless vast.

At the branch-tips spring has already stirred;
Grass and tree take on fresh color and breath.
In stillness I watch the turning of the hour —
The mind forgets the years still bound by taint.

Now and then I break a Baolin pine;
Then I draw water from Caoxi's stream,
And brew a tea amid the snow —
There is no taste to compare with this.

A thousand hills break through their wintry hue;
The earth's breath warms and brings forth spring.
Blossoms fall into Caoxi's water —
Who is willing to ask the ford?

With nothing to do, I doze by day;
The pine wind blows and never pierces through.
Whence comes that sound of the wooden fish?
In dream it rings out even stranger still.
Written Offhand

One drop of Caoxi's water;
A thousand pines that press the sky.
A man stands leaning on the bounds of space,
As if inside a painted scene.
To the Monks in Charge of Affairs: Two Poems

The snow before the cliff where the arm was cut —
Even now its blood runs thick.
The stone beneath the waist at Huangmei —
How many men can ever pound it?

Deep snow is bitter with congealing cold;
The grove is stripped and frozen through.
The moment a single yang begins to stir —
Spring is already betrayed at the branch-tips.
Dong Guobo Visits Caoxi, and So I Present This

One drop of Caoxi's water
Wanders across the rivers and lakes.
May it follow you as sweet rain,
And sprinkle the scorched and withered everywhere.
Wang Chi Visits on a Summer Day

The burning heat is poison, like fire;
The fragrance of tea is cold as ice.
Who knows that within this world of ours
All but the idle are outdone by a monk?
Farewell to Wuxin Rong, Chief Seat: Two Poems

A single flake of Jiangnan snow
Comes to cool the fever of the miasmal sea.
Now that you cross the ridge and go,
The chill of it clings to your brow.

A seven-foot staff clears overhead;
Three meals a day fill up the gourd.
When shall I, among ten thousand peaks,
Lie wearied, full, amid the clouds?
Facing the Moon

On the snow ridge a lone pine grows old;
In Caoxi a single drop runs cold.
Who knows that tonight's moon
Is still the same we watched of old?
Sailing Past Little Golden Mountain: Four Poems

Each time I come it is new once more;
Returning again, I never tire.
Only because I crave the Buddha's sun,
At times I bow to the Dharma King's own form.

The green hills never change their face;
The running water goes and comes again.
Only the moon amid the pines
Pours its clear light upon the moss.

The fishing lamps burn white in the deep of night;
The sand fowl clamor through the clear day.
The river is empty, the haunts of men are gone —
All day long the brushwood gate stays shut.

Below the steps fish and dragons rest at ease;
On the sandbar gulls and egrets take their leisure.
So brimming and full is this one stretch of water —
Yet it shuts off ten thousand ranges of hills.
Rejoicing That Huang Gongliang Has Returned from Jimen: Five Poems

No man's life reaches a hundred years;
Half of it was gone when first we met.
Then suddenly we parted three years more —
Who can reckon meeting and parting's debt?

Yesterday I rode a hollow boat;
In the night the wind and rain came down.
This morning I am overjoyed to meet you —
Far off and faint, as if in a dream.

On the frontier the grass-tips have turned white;
On Yan Mountain the maple leaves are red.
There is nothing left but the cold hue of snow,
And it still lingers on your brow.

Along the post road, a thousand rows of willow;
On rivers and lakes, ten thousand miles of wave.
Coming and going, the years are spent for nothing —
Who is it that has not idled them away?

The half-round moon over Luofu;
A single drop of Caoxi's water.
I share the taste of both with you —
There is no this or that in the flavor.
Rejoicing That Master Tanxin Qing Has Come

You have come down from the northern white,
To comfort me in this southern heat.
In the burning house we gladly look at one another —
As if facing the snows of Yan Mountain.
Inviting Master Qing to Taste Lychees

Through the long summer the fiery clouds are red;
In the fifth month the lychees ripen sweet.
I sit with you beside the Pearl River —
Day after day we tap the cold jade.
Facing Master Qing, Remembering Old Days

My hut once stood neighboring with yours;
We shared one love of water and bamboo.
Since we parted, thirty years have passed —
We look at each other, and now we are old.
Sent to the Two Princely Clans Zhen and Song of Puban and Xiangyuan: Three Poems

A single current of Yellow River water
Comes from far off in the heavens above.
On and on it flows east into the sea —
May I ask, when will it ever return?

The twin peaks of Hua Mountain stand forth;
In the high void the jade is cold.
Afar I hear the music of heaven ring —
It must be homage at the immortal altar.

The Zhongtiao Mountains are blue-green;
Morning clouds scatter bright brocade.
I know there is one who forgets the world,
Sitting alone to watch the Beginningless.
Dreaming a Visit to Tiantai: Two Poems

Suddenly I arrived at Tiantai Mountain,
And met an old man there among the clouds.
I think he must be one who fled the Qin —
His countenance is fair as this.

I flew up to the summit of Huading,
When suddenly I heard the heaven-cock crow.
Gazing far off toward Penglai Mountain,
I smoothed my beard and gave a long, long whistle.
Remembering Old Days

I dreamed I sat beneath the Dragon-Flower Tree,
And heard the Longyue bells ring out and die.
I woke within an empty valley —
A thousand ravines roared with the pine wind.
The Old Idle Monk Dwells in the Mountains

The hut is small; the hill hides a temple;
The heart is void; the mustard robe is bare.
Idly I sleep on the stone beneath the pine,
Sitting through the highest peak of all.
About to Go to Leiyang, I Take Leave of Master Tan on the River

We part beside the Hibiscus River;
Its waters in autumn are greener still.
The homeward boat goes up against the cold —
Coming and going, the heart is like woven thread.
In Praise of the Moon

On the clear sea its light seems to be;
In the cold sky its color seems to be gone.
Who knows that within a single glance
It has lit delusion's road for a thousand years?
In Praise of Clouds

A single speck, like a slender film;
Then spreading, it fills the whole vast void.
We know only that after it has risen —
We cannot see the hour before it was born.
Trying a Duan Inkstone: Three Poems

The noble man loves to wear jade,
Its warmth and mildness figuring his virtue.
This stone surpasses it even more —
Its true treasure lies in brush and ink.

The sea of words flows on ten thousand miles;
The brush's peak stands a thousand fathoms of snow.
All of it is born from within this stone —
Time and again it flies off in jade flakes.

Vast and boundless, the clear river water;
Piled and heaped, the purple stone mountain.
Who knows that the meaning of a thousand years
Lies from the first within the turbid blur?
Huacheng Hut: Two Poems

The mountain hues bring their own dusk and dawn;
The banyan's shade lies idle on the ancient road.
How many people come and go here —
The red dust stretches vast and empty on.

A well is dug upon the high plain;
The earth is deep, and water hard to find.
But when the work is carried to its utmost —
The deep spring flows and never stops.
The Chime-Stone Room

In a tiny room I hold a hidden gorge;
In poverty's company I meet the men of old.
Though I have but this inch-square patch of ground,
There is no place for clamorous dust to rest.
The Chan Devotee Ming Gives Tea

This mind from the first does not abide;
The barefoot one was never stained by dust.
From time to time he draws the fountainhead's water,
And cools the fevered, tormented in their heat.
Sent to Chentang, Chief Seat

I remember the place where you planted tea;
The whole garden soaked in spring rain.
When shall we sweep away the pine needles,
And face each other brewing a single cup?
Sent to Zongyuan of the West Hall

Caoxi's spring waters are rising;
The wild geese return to Heng Mountain.
I remember your nights of cross-legged sitting,
When the moon rose late over the pine gate.
Inscribed for the Chan Hall of Longxing Temple, Sent from Afar

The royal breath gathers in the mountains;
The sound of sutras reaches the imperial palace.
In the Dharma seat, a host of dragons and elephants —
For ten thousand ages we pray for the Yao wind.
Sent to Those Who Keep the Imperial Mausoleum Offerings

Heaven and earth opened the imperial enterprise;
Sun and moon turn the rivers and mountains about.
With incense and fire we serve the offerings diligently,
And morning and evening look up to the sacred face.
Inscribed on a Small Landscape Painting: Twenty-One Poems

Drifting clouds cover the spring hills;
A light cold freezes as if to split.
Whence does one come to tread the green?
When he returns, the moonlight is white.
